claim: XMAP215/Stu2/Alp14 proteins accelerate microtubule plus-end polymerization by recruiting tubulins via arrays of tumor overexpressed gene (TOG) domains.
source: XMAP215/Stu2/Alp14 proteins accelerate microtubule plus-end polymerization by recruiting tubulins via arrays of tumor overexpressed gene (TOG) domains, yet their mechanism remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about XMAP215/Stu2/Alp14 proteins.

claim: Alp14 binds four tubulins via dimeric TOG1-TOG2 subunits.
source: Alp14 binds four tubulins via dimeric TOG1-TOG2 subunits, in which each domain exhibits a distinct exchange rate for tubulin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Each TOG domain in Alp14 exhibits a distinct exchange rate for tubulin.
source: Alp14 binds four tubulins via dimeric TOG1-TOG2 subunits, in which each domain exhibits a distinct exchange rate for tubulin.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through biochemical experiments in Figure 1.

claim: X-ray structures revealed square-shaped assemblies composed of pseudo-dimeric TOG1-TOG2 subunits assembled head-to-tail.
source: X-ray structures revealed square-shaped assemblies composed of pseudo-dimeric TOG1-TOG2 subunits assembled head-to-tail, positioning four unpolymerized tubulins in a polarized wheel-like configuration.
evidence: This structural finding is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 2.

claim: TOG square assemblies position four unpolymerized tubulins in a polarized wheel-like configuration.
source: X-ray structures revealed square-shaped assemblies composed of pseudo-dimeric TOG1-TOG2 subunits assembled head-to-tail, positioning four unpolymerized tubulins in a polarized wheel-like configuration.
evidence: This is a structural observation stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: Crosslinking and electron microscopy show Alp14-tubulin forms square assemblies in solution.
source: Crosslinking and electron microscopy show Alp14-tubulin forms square assemblies in solution, and inactivating their interfaces destabilize this organization without influencing tubulin binding.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Inactivating TOG square interfaces destabilizes the organization without influencing tubulin binding.
source: Crosslinking and electron microscopy show Alp14-tubulin forms square assemblies in solution, and inactivating their interfaces destabilize this organization without influencing tubulin binding.
evidence: This is a finding from mutational analysis stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 4.

claim: An X-ray structure revealed an unfurled assembly in which TOG1-TOG2 uniquely bind to two polymerized tubulins.
source: An X-ray structure determined using approach to modulate tubulin polymerization revealed an unfurled assembly, in which TOG1-TOG2 uniquely bind to two polymerized tubulins.
evidence: This structural finding is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 5.

claim: TOG arrays recruit tubulins by forming square assemblies that then unfurl, facilitating their concerted polymerization into protofilaments.
source: Our findings suggest a new microtubule polymerase model in which TOG arrays recruit tubulins by forming square assemblies that then unfurl, facilitating their concerted polymerization into protofilaments.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic model proposed based on the structural and biochemical data presented.

claim: Microtubules are highly dynamic polarized polymers that perform critical and diverse cellular functions including formation of bipolar mitotic spindles, intracellular organization, and modulation of cell development and cell migration.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are highly dynamic polarized polymers that perform critical and diverse cellular functions including formation of bipolar mitotic spindles, intracellular organization, and modulation of cell development and cell migration (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2008; Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015).
evidence: This is established background knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: MTs are assembled from αβ-tubulin heterodimers.
source: MTs are assembled from αβ-tubulin heterodimers (herein termed αβ-tubulin), and their polymerization exhibits dynamic instability arising from guanosine triphosphate (GTP) hydrolysis in β-tubulins at MT ends.
evidence: This is established knowledge about microtubule structure.

claim: MT polymerization exhibits dynamic instability arising from GTP hydrolysis in β-tubulins at MT ends.
source: MTs are assembled from αβ-tubulin heterodimers (herein termed αβ-tubulin), and their polymerization exhibits dynamic instability arising from guanosine triphosphate (GTP) hydrolysis in β-tubulins at MT ends.
evidence: This is established knowledge about microtubule dynamics.

claim: The conformational changes promoting soluble αβ-tubulins to polymerize at MT ends remain poorly understood.
source: However, the conformational changes promoting soluble αβ-tubulins to polymerize at MT ends remain poorly understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: XMAP215/Stu2/Alp14 MT polymerases localize to the extreme tips of MT plus-ends and accelerate αβ-tubulin polymerization in eukaryotes.
source: The XMAP215/Stu2/Alp14 MT polymerases are among the best-studied families of MT regulators. They localize to the extreme tips of MT plus-ends and accelerate αβ-tubulin polymerization in eukaryotes (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2011; Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015; Al-Bassam and Chang, 2011; Maurer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Loss or depletion of MT polymerases is lethal in most eukaryotes as it severely decreases MT polymerization rates during interphase, resulting in shortened mitotic spindles.
source: Loss or depletion of MT polymerases is lethal in most eukaryotes as it severely decreases MT polymerization rates during interphase, resulting in shortened mitotic spindles (Al-Bassam et al., 2012; Cullen et al., 1999; Wang and Huffaker, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: MT polymerases bind kinetochores, where they accelerate MT dynamics and regulate kinetochore-MT attachment.
source: MT polymerases also bind kinetochores, where they accelerate MT dynamics and regulate kinetochore-MT attachment (Miller et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: MT polymerases recruit αβ-tubulins via arrays of conserved tumor overexpressed gene (TOG) domains, which are critical for their function.
source: MT polymerases recruit αβ-tubulins via arrays of conserved tumor overexpressed gene (TOG) domains (herein termed TOG arrays), which are critical for their function (Reber et al., 2013; Widlund et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Arrays of TOG-like domains are conserved in two other classes of MT regulators, CLASP and Crescerin/CHE-12 protein families.
source: Arrays of TOG-like domains are conserved in two other classes of MT regulators, CLASP and Crescerin/CHE-12 protein families (Al-Bassam and Chang, 2011; Al-Bassam et al., 2010; Das et al., 2015), suggesting that arrays of TOG domains uniquely evolved to regulate diverse MT polymerization functions through the binding of αβ-tubulins in various intracellular settings.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Yeast MT polymerases, such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae Stu2p and Schizosccharomyces pombe Alp14, are homodimers containing two unique and conserved TOG domain classes, TOG1 and TOG2, per subunit.
source: Yeast MT polymerases, such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae Stu2p and Schizosccharomyces pombe Alp14, are homodimers containing two unique and conserved TOG domain classes, TOG1 and TOG2, per subunit, numbered based on their proximity to the N-terminus in the protein sequence.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of yeast MT polymerases.

claim: Metazoan orthologs, such as XMAP215 and ch-TOG, are monomers with five tandem TOG domains, TOG1 through TOG5.
source: In contrast, metazoan orthologs, such as XMAP215 and ch-TOG, are monomers with five tandem TOG domains, TOG1 through TOG5 (Al-Bassam and Chang, 2011; Brouhard and Rice, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: TOG1 and TOG2 domains are evolutionarily distinct.
source: Phylogenetic analyses suggest that TOG1 and TOG2 domains are evolutionarily distinct (Al-Bassam and Chang, 2011), and that TOG3 and TOG4 domains in metazoans are evolutionarily and structurally exclusively related to the TOG1 and TOG2 domains, respectively (Brouhard et al., 2008; Fox et al., 2014; Howard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: TOG3 and TOG4 domains in metazoans are evolutionarily and structurally exclusively related to the TOG1 and TOG2 domains, respectively.
source: Phylogenetic analyses suggest that TOG1 and TOG2 domains are evolutionarily distinct (Al-Bassam and Chang, 2011), and that TOG3 and TOG4 domains in metazoans are evolutionarily and structurally exclusively related to the TOG1 and TOG2 domains, respectively (Brouhard et al., 2008; Fox et al., 2014; Howard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Both yeast and metazoan MT polymerases contain an array of tandem TOG1-TOG2 domains despite differences in TOG array organization.
source: Thus, despite differences in TOG array organization in yeast and metazoan proteins, both groups contain an array of tandem TOG1-TOG2 domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from phylogenetic analyses cited in the text.

claim: Each TOG domain is composed of six α-helical HEAT repeats, which form a conserved paddle-shaped structure.
source: Each TOG domain is composed of six α-helical HEAT (Huntingtin, EF3A, ATM, and TOR) repeats, which form a conserved paddle-shaped structure (Al-Bassam and Chang, 2011; Al-Bassam et al., 2007; Al-Bassam et al., 2006; Brouhard and Rice, 2014; Slep and Vale, 2007).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: X-ray structures of isolated TOG1 and TOG2 domains in complex with αβ-tubulins revealed that these domains recognize the curved αβ-tubulin conformations via inter-helical loops positioned along an edge of these paddle-shaped domains.
source: X-ray structures of isolated TOG1 and TOG2 domains in complex with αβ-tubulins revealed that these domains recognize the curved αβ-tubulin conformations via inter-helical loops positioned along an edge of these paddle-shaped domains (Ayaz et al., 2014; Ayaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Straightening of the curved αβ-tubulins upon polymerization into MTs likely dissociates TOG domains from the complexes.
source: Straightening of the curved αβ-tubulins upon polymerization into MTs likely dissociates TOG domains from the complexes.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on structural observations.

claim: Native TOG arrays from yeast or metazoan MT polymerases assemble into discrete particle-like assemblies upon binding αβ-tubulin.
source: Our previous studies indicate that native TOG arrays from yeast or metazoan MT polymerases assemble into discrete particle-like assemblies upon binding αβ-tubulin (Al-Bassam and Chang, 2011; Al-Bassam et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies by the authors.

claim: Both TOG1 and TOG2 domains are critical for MT polymerase function, and their inactivation results in MT functional defects.
source: Both TOG1 and TOG2 domains are critical for MT polymerase function, and their inactivation results in MT functional defects (Al-Bassam et al., 2012; Al-Bassam et al., 2006; Ayaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: 1 μM wt-Alp14-dimer binds four αβ-tubulins per dimer via its four TOG domains at 80-100 mM KCl.
source: We show that 1 μM wt-Alp14-dimer binds four αβ-tubulins per dimer via its four TOG domains (dimeric TOG1-TOG2 arrays), whereas 1 μM wt-Alp14-monomer binds two αβ-tubulins per dimer via two TOG domains.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 1 μM wt-Alp14-monomer binds two αβ-tubulins per monomer via two TOG domains at 80-100 mM KCl.
source: We show that 1 μM wt-Alp14-dimer binds four αβ-tubulins per dimer via its four TOG domains (dimeric TOG1-TOG2 arrays), whereas 1 μM wt-Alp14-monomer binds two αβ-tubulins per dimer via two TOG domains.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: TOG1 and TOG2 independently recruit αβ-tubulins.
source: Thus, TOG1 and TOG2 independently recruit αβ-tubulins (Figure 1A–B,D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C,D–F; Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: At 200 mM KCl, both 1 μM wt-Alp14-monomer and wt-Alp14-dimer bound roughly half as much αβ-tubulin than at 80–100 mM KCl.
source: At 200 mM KCl, both 1 μM wt-Alp14-monomer and wt-Alp14-dimer bound roughly half as much αβ-tubulin than at 80–100 mM KCl.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: TOG1M, which only includes two active TOG2 domains, bound two αβ-tubulins at 100 mM KCl, but almost completely dissociated from αβ-tubulin at 200 mM KCl.
source: 1 μM TOG1M, which only includes two active TOG2 domains, bound two αβ-tubulins at 100 mM KCl, but almost completely dissociated from αβ-tubulin at 200 mM KCl.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: TOG2M, which only includes two active TOG1 domains, bound and co-migrated with αβ-tubulin in both 100 and 200 mM KCl conditions.
source: In contrast, TOG2M, which only includes two active TOG1 domains, bound and co-migrated with αβ-tubulin in both 100 and 200 mM KCl conditions (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1J–L, Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: At 100 mM KCl, the dissociation constants for TOG1 and TOG2 were measured at 70 and 173 nM, respectively.
source: At 100 mM KCl, the dissociation constants for TOG1 and TOG2 were measured at 70 and 173 nM, respectively.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by ITC data in Figure 1E.

claim: At 200 mM KCl, TOG1 and TOG2 αβ-tubulin dissociation constants were measured at 1.5 μM and 3.2 μM, respectively.
source: However, at 200 mM KCl, we measured TOG1 and TOG2 αβ-tubulin dissociation constants at 1.5 μM and 3.2 μM, respectively, which showed 20-fold weaker affinity in absolute values compared to those measured at 100 mM KCl.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by ITC data in Figure 1E.

claim: DRP did not affect the simultaneous binding of multiple αβ-tubulins to TOG1-TOG2 arrays in either wt-Alp14-monomer or wt-Alp14-dimer.
source: We showed that DRP did not affect the simultaneous binding of multiple αβ-tubulins to TOG1-TOG2 arrays in either wt-Alp14-monomer or wt-Alp14-dimer.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by SEC-MALS data in Figure 1 supplement 2.

claim: The ability of Alp14-bound αβ-tubulin to bind stoichiometric amounts of DRP suggests that αβ-tubulins recruited by TOG arrays are in a non-polymerized state upon initial association with Alp14.
source: The ability of Alp14-bound αβ-tubulin to bind stoichiometric amounts of DRP suggests that αβ-tubulins recruited by TOG arrays are in a non-polymerized state upon initial association with Alp14.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the DRP binding data.

claim: The dimension of each wheel-like assembly was 210 × 198 × 60 Å.
source: The dimension of each wheel-like assembly was 210 × 198 × 60 Å (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the X-ray structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The 2:4:4 stoichiometry observed in the X-ray structure matched the stoichiometry measured for wt-Alp14-dimer:αβ-tubulin:DRP complexes.
source: The 2:4:4 stoichiometry observed in the X-ray structure matched the stoichiometry measured for wt-Alp14-dimer:αβ-tubulin:DRP complexes (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This comparison between structural and biochemical data is stated in the text.

claim: In a TOG square, each TOG domain was bound to a curved αβ-tubulin capped by a DRP through its outward-facing binding interface and was not in contact with the neighboring TOG-bound αβ-tubulin.
source: In a TOG square, each TOG domain was bound to a curved αβ-tubulin capped by a DRP through its outward-facing binding interface and was not in contact with the neighboring TOG-bound αβ-tubulin (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the X-ray structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The β-tubulin on a TOG1-bound αβ-tubulin is rotated approximately 90° from its polymer-forming interface relative to the adjacent α-tubulin on a TOG2-bound αβ-tubulin.
source: The β-tubulin on a TOG1-bound αβ-tubulin is rotated approximately 90° from its polymer-forming interface relative to the adjacent α-tubulin on a TOG2-bound αβ-tubulin (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the X-ray structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: Interface 1 packs a 668 Å2 surface area and positions the TOG1 C-terminus at 90° to a 10-residue segment of the TOG1-TOG2 linker and the N-terminus of TOG2.
source: Interface 1 packs a 668 Å2 surface area and positions the TOG1 C-terminus at 90° to a 10-residue segment of the TOG1-TOG2 linker and the N-terminus of TOG2.
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the X-ray structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: Interface 2 packs a 290 Å2 surface area and positions the TOG2 C-terminus at 90° to the N-terminus of TOG1.
source: Interface 2 packs a 290 Å2 surface area and positions the TOG2 C-terminus at 90° to the N-terminus of TOG1 (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the X-ray structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The total buried surface area stabilizing two sets of interfaces 1 and 2 in a TOG square is 1930 Å2.
source: The total buried surface area stabilizing two sets of interfaces 1 and 2 in a TOG square is 1930 Å2, which is moderate in size and dispersed for such a large assembly.
evidence: This is a structural measurement calculated from the X-ray structure.

claim: Mass spectrometry confirmed that the 170 kDa intermediate was indeed the sk-Alp14-S180C-L304C protein.
source: Mass spectrometry confirmed that this 170 kDa intermediate was indeed the sk-Alp14-S180C-L304C protein.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 3.

claim: Peptide disulfide mapping revealed only two classes of peptides in sk-Alp14-S180C-L304C with 105 Da of mass added onto the cysteines, suggesting that they were engaged in disulfide bonds with the following sequence boundaries: 297–320 and 179–189.
source: This approach revealed only two classes of peptides in sk-Alp14-S180C-L304C with 105 Da of mass added onto the cysteines, suggesting that they were engaged in disulfide bonds with the following sequence boundaries: 297–320 and 179–189 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 3 supplement 1.

claim: These data directly provide independent support of interface 1 of the TOG square conformation forming in sk-Alp14-dimer in solution outside of the crystallographic setting.
source: Thus, these data directly provide independent support of interface 1 of the TOG square conformation forming in sk-Alp14-dimer in solution outside of the crystallographic setting, and of indeed being the inter-subunit dimeric interface between two TOG-array subunits, as visualized in the crystal structures (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the crosslinking and mass spectrometry data.

claim: INT1, INT2, and INT1 +2 mutants bound nearly identical quantities of αβ-tubulin to wt-Alp14-dimer.
source: INT1, INT2, and INT1 +2 mutants bound nearly identical quantities of αβ-tubulin to wt-Alp14-dimer (Figure 4E; Figure 4F,G,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by SEC-MALS data in Figure 4.

claim: INT1, INT2, and INT1 +2 bound approximately four αβ-tubulins at 80 mM KCl as assessed by SEC-MALS.
source: INT1, INT2, and INT1 +2 bound approximately four αβ-tubulins at 80 mM KCl as assessed by SEC-MALS (Tables 1 and 2; Figure 4F,G,H) and approximately half of the bound αβ-tubulin dissociated at 200 mM KCl as quantitated by quantitative-SEC (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E,F).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by SEC-MALS data in Figure 4.

claim: Approximately half of the αβ-tubulin bound to INT1, INT2, and INT1+2 dissociated at 200 mM KCl.
source: INT1, INT2, and INT1 +2 bound approximately four αβ-tubulins at 80 mM KCl as assessed by SEC-MALS (Tables 1 and 2; Figure 4F,G,H) and approximately half of the bound αβ-tubulin dissociated at 200 mM KCl as quantitated by quantitative-SEC (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E,F).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by quantitative-SEC data in Figure 4.

claim: 4:2 wt-Alp14-dimer:αβ-tubulin complexes formed two types compact particle-like assemblies of either 15 or 19 nm diameter compact circular complexes.
source: Negative stain images showed that 4:2 wt-Alp14-dimer:αβ-tubulin complexes formed two types compact particle-like assemblies of either 15 or 19 nm diameter compact circular complexes (Figure 2) matched the general features previously described for yeast Stu2p-tubulin or XMAP215-tubulin we previously described (Al-Bassam et al., 2006; Brouhard et al., 2008).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by negative stain EM data in Figure 4.

claim: TOG square bound to four αβ-tubulins matched well the density organization of the 19 nm diameter 2D-class averages.
source: 2D-image class averages were compared via projection-matching to low resolution-filtered structural models for a TOG square with and without four αβ-tubulins, revealing TOG square bound to four αβ-tubulins matched well the density organization of the 19 nm diameter 2D-class averages (Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by EM data in Figure 4.

claim: INT1:αβ-tubulin complexes did not form square assemblies, and particles exhibited either open flexible organization with many inter-connected 8 nm long inter-connected densities or 16 nm long short filaments.
source: In contrast, INT1:αβ-tubulin complexes did not form square assemblies, and particles exhibited either open flexible organization with many inter-connected 8 nm long inter-connected densities or 16 nm long short filaments.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by EM data in Figure 4.

claim: INT1 +2 αβ-tubulin complexes showed only dissociated, flexibly connected necklaces of 8 nm densities of αβ-tubulin.
source: While, INT1 +2 αβ-tubulin complexes showed only dissociated, flexibly connected necklaces of 8 nm densities of αβ-tubulin (Figure 4L).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by EM data in Figure 4.

claim: DRPΔN affinity for αβ-tubulin showed a three-fold decrease compared to DRP.
source: We measured DRPΔN affinity using ITC, revealing a three-fold decrease in its αβ-tubulin-binding affinity as compared to DRP (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by ITC data in Figure 5.

claim: The refined 3.2 Å 1:2:1 X-ray structure revealed an extended conformation with two αβ-tubulins polymerized head-to-tail in a curved protofilament.
source: The refined 3.2 Å 1:2:1 X-ray structure revealed an extended conformation with two αβ-tubulins polymerized head-to-tail in a curved protofilament (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the X-ray structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the unfurled conformation, TOG1 and TOG2 did not form any interactions with each other and their adjoining linker became disordered.
source: In this conformation, TOG1 and TOG2 did not form any interactions with each other and their adjoining linker became disordered (Figure 5E,F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the X-ray structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: TOG1 and TOG2 were specifically bound to the lower and upper αβ-tubulins, respectively, of a highly curved protofilament.
source: TOG1 and TOG2 were specifically bound to the lower and upper αβ-tubulins, respectively, of a highly curved protofilament.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the X-ray structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: Only a single DRPΔN capped the TOG2-bound αβ-tubulin in the unfurled structure.
source: Only a single DRPΔN capped the TOG2-bound αβ-tubulin (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the X-ray structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: The unfurling rearrangement required 68°-rotation and 32 Å translation of TOG2:αβ-tubulin hinging around interface 2 and TOG1-αβ-tubulin.
source: Compared to the TOG square, this 'unfurling' rearrangement required 68°-rotation and 32 Å translation of TOG2:αβ-tubulin hinging around interface 2 and TOG1-αβ-tubulin (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a structural comparison between the TOG square and unfurled structures shown in Figure 6.

claim: The two αβ-tubulin polymers in the unfurled complex were highly curved protofilaments with 16.4° inter-dimer interface.
source: The two αβ-tubulin polymers in this complex were highly curved protofilaments (16.4° inter-dimer interface).
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the X-ray structure.

claim: The protofilament structure displayed ~3° more curvature than RB3/stathmin-αβ-tubulin curved protofilament structures.
source: This protofilament structure displayed ~3° more curvature than RB3/stathmin-αβ-tubulin curved protofilament structures (Table 4; Figure 5—figure supplement 2E) (Nawrotek et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a structural comparison stated in the text and shown in Figure 5 supplement 2.

claim: Polymerization is associated with a 5° rotation and 10 Å translation in the T7 loop and H8 helix of the TOG2-bound α-tubulin.
source: Comparison of the αβ-tubulin dimer structure (α2β2) within this 1:2:1 structure to the unpolymerized αβ-tubulin structure revealed that polymerization is associated with a 5° rotation and 10 Å translation in the T7 loop and H8 helix of the TOG2-bound α-tubulin, which engages TOG1-bound β-tubulin elements and the E-site-bound GDP nucleotide (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: No steric contact was observed when the TOG square was docked via αβ-tubulin-TOG2.
source: In contrast, we observed no steric contact when the TOG square was docked via αβ-tubulin-TOG2.
evidence: This is an observation from molecular modeling shown in Figure 7.

claim: The destabilization of the TOG squares is more likely if TOG1-αβ-tubulin docks onto the protofilament plus-end in contrast to TOG2-αβ-tubulin docking.
source: These differences suggest that the destabilization of the TOG squares is more likely if TOG1-αβ-tubulin docks onto the protofilament plus-end in contrast to TOG2-αβ-tubulin docking.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the molecular modeling results.

claim: Upon recruiting four soluble αβ-tubulins, dimeric TOG1-TOG2 arrays in proteins such Alp14 or Stu2, organize into compact TOG square assemblies in solution.
source: Upon recruiting four soluble αβ-tubulins, dimeric TOG1-TOG2 arrays in proteins such Alp14 or Stu2, organize into compact TOG square assemblies in solution (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a step in the proposed model shown in Figure 8.

claim: TOG square assemblies place αβ-tubulins in close proximity with each other in a near head-to-tail polarized orientation while inhibiting spontaneous polymerization.
source: These assemblies place αβ-tubulins in close proximity with each other in a near head-to-tail polarized while inhibiting spontaneous polymerization.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on structural data.

claim: The αβ-tubulin-loaded TOG square assemblies diffuse along the MT lattice, mediated by an interaction of the SK-rich regions immediately C-terminal to TOG2, with acidic tubulin C-termini exposed on MT surfaces.
source: The αβ-tubulin-loaded TOG square assemblies diffuse along the MT lattice, mediated by an interaction of the SK-rich regions immediately C-terminal to TOG2, with acidic tubulin C-termini exposed on MT surfaces (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a step in the proposed model shown in Figure 8.

claim: Proximity of the SK-rich region to the TOG array is essential for MT polymerase activity.
source: Proximity of the SK-rich region to the TOG array is essential for MT polymerase activity, and increasing its polypeptide distance causes MT polymerase defects (Geyer et al., 2018; Al-Bassam et al., 2012; Brouhard et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: TOG squares docking to protofilament ends via TOG1-αβ-tubulin destabilizes the TOG square in contrast with TOG2:αβ-tubulin, which will not destabilize the TOG square at protofilament tips.
source: Thus, TOG squares docking to protofilament ends via TOG1-αβ-tubulin destabilizes the TOG square in contrast with TOG2:αβ-tubulin, which will not destabilize the TOG square at protofilament tips, leading to selection of TOG1 at the docking site (Figurer 8B-II).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on structural modeling.

claim: The MT plus-end-induced TOG square destabilization likely triggers TOG square disassembly into two corner-shaped TOG1-TOG2 subunits at MT plus-ends.
source: The MT plus-end-induced TOG square destabilization likely triggers TOG square disassembly into two corner-shaped TOG1-TOG2 subunits at MT plus-ends.
evidence: This is a step in the proposed model based on structural data.

claim: Interface 2 likely acts as a flexible hinge for TOG2 to freely rotate around TOG1, driven by Brownian motion.
source: Corner-like half-square TOG1-TOG2 subunit assemblies are then released which are likely unstable (Figure 8B–II), and interface 2 likely acts as a flexible hinge for TOG2 to freely rotate around TOG1, driven by Brownian motion.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal in the model based on structural data.

claim: Reversible unfurling, or hinge rotation, promotes αβ-tubulin bound to TOG2 to polymerize catalytically onto the plus-end of the TOG1-bound αβ-tubulin.
source: Reversible unfurling, or hinge rotation, promotes αβ-tubulin bound to TOG2 to polymerize catalytically onto the plus-end of the TOG1-bound αβ-tubulin (Figure 8B–III).
evidence: This is a step in the proposed model shown in Figure 8.
